sentences.text: Revenue, net interest income plus noninterest income, rose from $20,956 million in FY2016 to $28,540 million in FY2025 [D5][D219], a 3.5% CAGR.
The path was a step change, not a compounder: revenue was $22,883 million in FY2019 [D66] and $28,013 million in FY2023 [D169], with the MUB acquisition lifting FY2023 revenue 15.8% [D189].
The FY2023 jump reflected an 18.1% increase in net interest income and a 12.3% increase in noninterest income, the former due to higher rates on earning assets and the MUB acquisition [P33].

FY2024 reversed 2.4% [D214] as net interest income fell 6.4% on higher rates pressuring deposit mix and pricing [P21], before FY2025 recovered 4.4% [D239] on loan growth and lower deposit rates [P16].
Consumer and Business Banking was the largest segment at 31.0% of revenue in FY2025 [D251], but it shrank 3.9% and subtracted 1.3pp from growth [D252][D253].
That decline came from a 4.9% fall in segment net interest income on deposit mix changes and second-quarter loan sales [P6].
Payment Services grew 5.4% in FY2025 [D260], contributing 1.4pp [D261] on 25.8% of revenue [D259].
Payment Services net revenue rose 5.4% on higher loan balances and lower funding costs, with noninterest income up on merchant processing and card volume [P4].
Net income grew 20.2% in FY2025 [D227] against 4.4% revenue growth [D239], and EPS rose 21.9% [D229] with the diluted share count down 0.2% [D237].
The efficiency ratio was 59.0% in FY2025 [D220], below its 59.3% window median [D277] and far under the 67.4% FY2023 high [D276], and better than the 61.7% peer median [D281].
Noninterest expense fell 2.0% in FY2025 [D238] on prior-year merger and FDIC special assessment charges, lower compensation and higher technology spend [P10].
The credit-loss provision was 7.7% of revenue in FY2025 [D221], above the 6.1% peer median [D285], though the provision itself fell 2.3% [P12].
Net margin was 26.5% in FY2025 [D223] against a 20.2% effective tax rate [D215], leaving net margin close to operating margin.
For a bank, operating cash flow is not a meaningful earnings-quality measure; capital return is the better test.
Operating cash flow was $7,970 million in FY2025, 1.05x net income [F60][D216], down 29.8% [D230] from the 1.80x of FY2024 [D191].
Buybacks plus dividends of $3,657 million [D218] covered 48.3% of FY2025 net income of $7,570 million [F30].
Return on average equity was 12.2% in FY2025 [D226], above the 11.8% peer median [D283] and in the 71st percentile of seven banks [D282].
Loans were 73.5% of deposits [D224] and the allowance was 2.0% of loans [D225], with equity up 11.3% to $65,193 million [D233][F114].
Buybacks fell to $489 million in FY2025 [X85] from $4,525 million in FY2019 [X79], while dividends rose to $3,168 million [X95].
The diluted share count fell 0.2% in FY2025 [D237] after rising 3.6% in FY2023 [D187] on MUB-related issuance.
Revenue declined 2.4% in FY2024 [D194], the one flagged candidate [R1], driven by a 6.4% fall in net interest income on deposit mix and pricing [P21].
The decline proved short-lived: revenue rose 4.4% in FY2025 [D239], so the flag is a single-period rate-cycle effect rather than a persistent trend.
Consumer and Business Banking net income fell to $1,723 million in FY2025 [S7] from $2,500 million in FY2023 [S5], a two-year slide worth watching.
Efficiency ratio: a move back above the 59.3% window median [D277] would reverse the FY2025 cost improvement, visible in the FY2026 10-K.
Net interest income: holding above the FY2025 level of $16,649 million [F10] would confirm the FY2025 recovery; a drop back toward the FY2024 $16,289 million [F9] would not.
Consumer and Business Banking net income: a further fall below the FY2025 $1,723 million [S7] would extend the two-year decline.
